notes.deck: Agile Architecture::01 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Way of Thinking
notes.front: What is the Open Agile Architecture (O-AA) Standard?
notes.back: A standard of The Open Group describing how to architect at scale with agility: guidance for enterprises that run a Digital Transformation and an Agile Transformation together.
notes.extra: First published September 2020 (corrigendum reissue October 2022); Version 2.0 published April 2026.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 1: The Agile Way of Thinking

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::01 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Way of Thinking
notes.text:
Version 2.0 of the standard has four parts:
Part 1: {{c1::The Agile Way of Thinking}}
Part 2: {{c2::The Agile Enterprise}}
Part 3: {{c3::The Agile Architecture Capability}}
Part 4: {{c4::The Ways of Supporting}}
notes.extra: Why (thinking), who and where (enterprise), how architecture works (capability), with what techniques (supporting).
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 1: The Agile Way of Thinking

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::01 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Way of Thinking
notes.front: What is the dual transformation the standard is built around?
notes.back: A Digital Transformation and an Agile Transformation pursued in a coordinated way, because each one enables and reinforces the other.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 1: The Agile Way of Thinking

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::01 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Way of Thinking
notes.front: In the standard's dual transformation, what does Digital Transformation change?
notes.back:
It uses digital technology to reshape four things:
  • strategy
  • product
  • the operating system (how the enterprise operates)
  • the experience of customers, employees and other stakeholders
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 1: The Agile Way of Thinking

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::01 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Way of Thinking
notes.front: In the standard's dual transformation, what does Agile Transformation develop?
notes.back: The organisational and cultural capacity to notice change early and respond to it quickly and decisively.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 1: The Agile Way of Thinking

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::01 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Way of Thinking
notes.front: Why does the standard insist that Digital and Agile Transformation be pursued together?
notes.back: They co-create each other: more agility gives faster learning cycles, faster learning shortens time-to-market, and digital capabilities in turn make the enterprise more agile.
notes.extra: Digital technology on top of a slow, siloed organisation delivers slowly; agility without digital capability has little to deliver with.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 1: The Agile Way of Thinking

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::01 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Way of Thinking
notes.front: What goes wrong when Agile is scaled without architecture?
notes.back: Autonomous teams optimise locally: duplicated solutions, inconsistent customer experience, tightly coupled systems and growing integration and technical debt, which end up slowing every team down.
notes.extra: The standard's premise: efforts to deploy Agile at scale are too often made at the expense of architecture.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 1: The Agile Way of Thinking

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::01 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Way of Thinking
notes.front: What does Agile Architecture aim at, in two senses?
notes.back:
1. Architecting in an Agile way: architecture practice that complements and enables Agile ways of working at scale instead of gating them.
  2. An architecture that is itself agile: modular, loosely coupled and evolvable, so it can change cheaply as the enterprise learns.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 1: The Agile Way of Thinking

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::01 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Way of Thinking
notes.front: How wide is the scope of architecture in the standard?
notes.back:
Far wider than Information Technology (IT). It spans
  • strategy and business model
  • customer experience
  • product
  • operations (the 'operating system')
  • organisation
  • software, data and technology
notes.extra: This is why the standard addresses business leaders, product managers and operations managers, not only architects.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 1: The Agile Way of Thinking

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::01 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Way of Thinking
notes.front: In the standard, what does operating system mean?
notes.back: The enterprise's operations system: everything (assets, processes, people) that works together to deliver its products and services.
notes.extra: Lean usage of the term. It is not a computer operating system.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 1: The Agile Way of Thinking

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::01 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Way of Thinking
notes.front: Which three audiences does Version 2.0 name?
notes.back:
• Agilists who need to see why architecture matters at scale and want architecture skills
  • Architects (enterprise, solution, security, software) who need new skills for an Agile-at-scale, digital context
  • Business managers, executives and technical leaders who need to influence architecture decisions
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 1: The Agile Way of Thinking

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::01 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Way of Thinking
notes.front: How does the standard relate to The Open Group Architecture Framework (TOGAF) Standard?
notes.back: It complements it rather than replacing it: it addresses the architectural challenges of Agile at scale and Digital Transformation, and can be used alongside TOGAF.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 1: The Agile Way of Thinking

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::01 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Way of Thinking
notes.front: Why is modularity the central structural idea of Agile Architecture?
notes.back: A modular system is split into loosely coupled parts with well-defined interfaces, so each part can be changed, replaced or scaled independently. That independence is what lets teams work autonomously.
notes.extra: The standard applies modularity three times over: to the product, to the organisation and to the software.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 1: The Agile Way of Thinking

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::01 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Way of Thinking
notes.front: What is evolvability?
notes.back: The ability of a system to accommodate change over time at low cost and risk, without having to be redesigned from scratch.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 1: The Agile Way of Thinking

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::01 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Way of Thinking
notes.front: What does it mean to apply systems thinking to the enterprise?
notes.back: Treat the enterprise as a whole socio-technical system: look at the interactions between parts (people, processes, technology) and optimise the whole, not each part in isolation.
notes.extra: Local optimisation of a function or team often degrades end-to-end flow.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 1: The Agile Way of Thinking

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::01 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Way of Thinking
notes.front: Why is alignment a precondition for team autonomy rather than its opposite?
notes.back: Teams can only be left to decide for themselves when they share intent, boundaries and interfaces. Without alignment, autonomy produces divergence; without autonomy, alignment produces bureaucracy.
notes.extra: Architecture is one of the main alignment mechanisms: it defines boundaries, interfaces and guardrails.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 1: The Agile Way of Thinking

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::01 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Way of Thinking
notes.front: How does the standard use the word product?
notes.back: A bundle of services and/or goods offered to customers. It is the unit around which experience, teams, funding and architecture are organised.
notes.extra: Broader than a software product: it can be a physical good, a service or a combination.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 1: The Agile Way of Thinking

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::01 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Way of Thinking
notes.front: What is a platform business model?
notes.back: A business model that creates value by enabling exchanges between two or more interdependent groups (for example producers and consumers), drawing on two-sided market effects.
notes.extra: Distinct from a digital platform, which is the reconfigurable software and infrastructure foundation teams build on.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 1: The Agile Way of Thinking

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::01 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Way of Thinking
notes.front: What is an outcome, as opposed to an output?
notes.back: An output is what a team produces (a feature, a release). An outcome is the resulting change for the customer or the business. Agile architecture steers by outcomes.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 1: The Agile Way of Thinking

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::01 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Way of Thinking
notes.front: What does it mean to treat a strategic or design choice as a hypothesis?
notes.back: State it as an assumption that could be wrong, define the evidence that would confirm or refute it, and test it with the cheapest experiment before committing at scale.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 1: The Agile Way of Thinking

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::02 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Enterprise
notes.front: Which four topics make up Part 2 (The Agile Enterprise) in Version 2.0?
notes.back:
• Organisational structures (including team taxonomies)
  • Agile strategy
  • Architecting the Agile Transformation
  • Agile governance
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 2: The Agile Enterprise

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::02 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Enterprise
notes.front: What characterises an Agile organisation in the standard?
notes.back:
• small, autonomous, cross-functional teams
  • teams aligned with value streams, not functions
  • decision authority pushed to where the information is
  • short feedback loops with customers and operations
  • a few shared operating principles instead of heavy central coordination
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 2: The Agile Enterprise

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::02 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Enterprise
notes.text: Version 2.0's team taxonomy has three kinds of team: {{c1::stream-aligned}}, {{c2::platform}} and {{c3::competency}} teams.
notes.extra: Compare with Team Topologies' four: stream-aligned, platform, enabling, complicated-subsystem.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 2: The Agile Enterprise

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::02 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Enterprise
notes.front: What is a stream-aligned team?
notes.back: A cross-functional team aligned to a single stream of value (a product, service, customer journey or segment), able to deliver end to end without hand-offs to other teams.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 2: The Agile Enterprise

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::02 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Enterprise
notes.front: What is a platform team?
notes.back: A team that provides internal services, tooling and infrastructure as a self-service product, so stream-aligned teams can deliver autonomously without building those foundations themselves.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 2: The Agile Enterprise

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::02 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Enterprise
notes.front: What is a competency team in the Version 2.0 team taxonomy?
notes.back: A team that concentrates scarce expertise and makes it available to other teams, raising their capability rather than delivering the value stream itself.
notes.extra: Roughly the role Team Topologies gives to enabling teams.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 2: The Agile Enterprise

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::02 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Enterprise
notes.front: Feature team versus component team: what is the difference?
notes.back: A feature team is cross-functional and delivers customer-visible functionality across all components it touches. A component team owns one technical component or layer, so a feature needs several teams and hand-offs.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 2: The Agile Enterprise

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::02 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Enterprise
notes.front: How does Agile strategy differ from classic strategic planning?
notes.back: Strategy becomes a continuous loop of formulating, deploying and learning, expressed as choices and hypotheses that are tested and revised, instead of a periodic plan cascaded top-down and executed as written.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 2: The Agile Enterprise

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::02 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Enterprise
notes.front: What is catchball?
notes.back: A strategy deployment practice from Hoshin Kanri: objectives and the means to reach them are passed back and forth between levels of the organisation until both sides agree, instead of being cascaded one way.
notes.extra: The image is a ball thrown back and forth.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 2: The Agile Enterprise

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::02 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Enterprise
notes.front: What are Objectives and Key Results (OKRs)?
notes.back: A goal-setting practice: a qualitative Objective stating what to achieve, with a few measurable Key Results showing whether it was achieved.
notes.extra: Key Results should measure outcomes, not list tasks. Originated at Intel (Andy Grove), popularised by John Doerr.
notes.source: Doerr, Measure What Matters (2018) · Open Agile Architecture / Part 2: The Agile Enterprise

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::02 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Enterprise
notes.front: Why does an Agile Transformation have to be architected, not just rolled out?
notes.back: It changes the enterprise's social system (structures, roles, decision rights, behaviours, beliefs), not only its processes. That needs a designed target, an evolutionary path and feedback, like any other architecture.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 2: The Agile Enterprise

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::02 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Enterprise
notes.front: What is meant by the enterprise's social system?
notes.back: People and how they work together: organisation structure, roles, decision rights, norms, culture, beliefs and skills. It is designed jointly with the technical system.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 2: The Agile Enterprise

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::02 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Enterprise
notes.front: What shift in leadership does an Agile Transformation require?
notes.back: From command-and-control (deciding and directing) to setting intent and context, distributing decision authority, and removing impediments for teams.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 2: The Agile Enterprise

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::02 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Enterprise
notes.front: Why do big-bang Agile Transformations tend to fail, and what is the alternative?
notes.back: They change structure and labels faster than mental models and capabilities can follow. The alternative is incremental: start with selected value streams, learn, then extend.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 2: The Agile Enterprise

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::02 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Enterprise
notes.front: How does Agile governance differ from traditional governance?
notes.back:
It shifts from stage gates, up-front approvals and after-the-fact compliance checks to
  • guardrails within which teams decide themselves
  • automated, continuous verification
  • authority delegated to the level that holds the information
  • transparency through shared metrics instead of status reporting
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 2: The Agile Enterprise

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::02 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Enterprise
notes.front: What is a guardrail?
notes.back: A boundary condition (a constraint, policy or standard) within which teams are free to make their own decisions. It prevents harmful outcomes without prescribing the solution.
notes.extra: Example: 'services expose data only through versioned Application Programming Interfaces (APIs)'.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 2: The Agile Enterprise

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::02 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Enterprise
notes.front: Reversible versus irreversible decisions: how should each be governed?
notes.back: Irreversible (one-way door) decisions deserve deliberate, careful analysis. Reversible (two-way door) decisions should be made quickly by the people closest to the work.
notes.extra: Amazon's Type 1 / Type 2 distinction. Applying heavyweight process to reversible decisions is a common cause of slowness.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 2: The Agile Enterprise

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::02 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Enterprise
notes.front: What does it mean to automate governance?
notes.back: Encode policies, standards and architectural rules as executable checks (tests, pipeline gates, policy-as-code) so compliance is verified continuously on every change instead of by review boards.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 2: The Agile Enterprise

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::03 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Architecture Capability
notes.front: How is Part 3 (The Agile Architecture Capability) subdivided in Version 2.0?
notes.back:
• Part 3A, Architecture Development Style: intentional architecture and continuous architectural refactoring
  • Part 3B, Architecture Deliverables: operations architecture, product architecture, software architecture, and DevOps / Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) practices
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 3: The Agile Architecture Capability

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::03 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Architecture Capability
notes.text: The standard combines two architecture development styles: {{c1::intentional architecture}} and {{c2::continuous architectural refactoring}}.
notes.extra: Deliberate direction plus emergence. Neither is sufficient alone.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 3: The Agile Architecture Capability

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::03 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Architecture Capability
notes.front: What is intentional architecture?
notes.back: Architecture that is deliberately planned: decisions, models and statements of direction describing a target state the enterprise steers towards.
notes.extra: It gives direction across teams; it is not a detailed up-front design.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 3: The Agile Architecture Capability

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::03 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Architecture Capability
notes.front: What is continuous architectural refactoring?
notes.back: Improving the structure of an architecture in small, frequent steps while the system stays in operation, so the architecture emerges and keeps its ability to evolve.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 3: The Agile Architecture Capability

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::03 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Architecture Capability
notes.front: Why is purely emergent architecture insufficient at scale?
notes.back: A single team can evolve its design by refactoring, but concerns that cut across teams (shared boundaries, interfaces, platforms, data, security) do not emerge from local decisions.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 3: The Agile Architecture Capability

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::03 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Architecture Capability
notes.front: Why is purely up-front architecture insufficient?
notes.back: It fixes decisions when knowledge is lowest. In an uncertain, fast-changing context those decisions are overtaken by what the enterprise learns from customers and operations.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 3: The Agile Architecture Capability

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::03 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Architecture Capability
notes.front: What does it mean that architecture development is concurrent and continuous?
notes.back: Architecture work runs in parallel with product discovery and delivery, by people embedded in or close to the teams, instead of being a phase that finishes before delivery starts.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 3: The Agile Architecture Capability

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::03 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Architecture Capability
notes.front: What is Set-Based Concurrent Engineering (SBCE)?
notes.back: Developing several design options in parallel and eliminating the weaker ones as evidence accumulates, instead of committing early to a single point design.
notes.extra: From Toyota's product development. It delays commitment to the point where knowledge is highest.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 3: The Agile Architecture Capability

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::03 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Architecture Capability
notes.front: What is an architectural runway?
notes.back: The technical foundation already in place (code, components, infrastructure) that allows upcoming features to be built without first stopping for major redesign.
notes.extra: Too short a runway and teams stall on rework; too long and you are speculating.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 3: The Agile Architecture Capability

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::03 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Architecture Capability
notes.front: What is refactoring?
notes.back: Changing the internal structure of software to make it easier to understand and cheaper to modify, without changing its observable behaviour.
notes.source: Fowler, Refactoring (2nd ed., 2018) · Open Agile Architecture / Part 3: The Agile Architecture Capability

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::03 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Architecture Capability
notes.front: What is a fitness function in evolutionary architecture?
notes.back: An objective, preferably automated, check of how well the architecture meets a desired characteristic (performance, coupling, security, resilience). It protects that characteristic as the system changes.
notes.extra: Example: a build step that fails when a module imports from a forbidden layer.
notes.source: Ford, Parsons, Kua, Building Evolutionary Architectures (2017) · Open Agile Architecture / Part 3: The Agile Architecture Capability

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::03 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Architecture Capability
notes.front: Which preconditions make continuous architectural refactoring feasible?
notes.back:
• comprehensive automated tests
  • continuous integration and continuous delivery
  • loosely coupled, modular components
  • fitness functions and guardrails
  • teams that own their code and are allowed time to improve it
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 3: The Agile Architecture Capability

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::03 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Architecture Capability
notes.front: What is technical debt?
notes.back: The future cost of rework caused by choosing an expedient solution now. Like financial debt, it accrues interest: every later change in that area costs more until the debt is repaid.
notes.extra: Metaphor coined by Ward Cunningham (1992).
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 3: The Agile Architecture Capability

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::03 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Architecture Capability
notes.text: Part 3B names four areas of architecture deliverables: {{c1::operations}} architecture, {{c2::product}} architecture, {{c3::software}} architecture, and {{c4::DevOps / Site Reliability Engineering}} practices.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 3: The Agile Architecture Capability

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::03 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Architecture Capability
notes.front: What is product architecture?
notes.back: How a product's functions are allocated to its components, and how those components interface with each other.
notes.extra: Ulrich (1995). Applies to physical goods, services and digital products.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 3: The Agile Architecture Capability

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::03 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Architecture Capability
notes.front: Modular versus integral product architecture: what is the trade-off?
notes.back: Modular: each function maps to one component with decoupled interfaces; easy to change and vary, at some cost in global optimisation. Integral: functions spread across tightly coupled components; can be optimised as a whole but is hard to change.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 3: The Agile Architecture Capability

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::03 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Architecture Capability
notes.front: What is a product platform?
notes.back: A set of assets (components, processes, knowledge) shared across a family of products, from which variants can be derived efficiently.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 3: The Agile Architecture Capability

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::03 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Architecture Capability
notes.front: What does operations architecture design?
notes.back: The enterprise's operating system: the value streams, processes, capacity and supporting technology that deliver products and services, designed for flow, quality and short lead times.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 3: The Agile Architecture Capability

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::03 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Architecture Capability
notes.front: Two meanings of value stream are in use. What are they?
notes.back:
• Lean value stream: all the actions, value-adding or not, needed to bring a product from concept to launch or from order to delivery; mapped to find waste and improve flow.
  • Value stream in business architecture: the end-to-end set of activities that produces a result of value for a customer or stakeholder.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 3: The Agile Architecture Capability

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::03 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Architecture Capability
notes.front: What is hexagonal architecture (ports and adapters)?
notes.back: A style that isolates domain logic at the centre. The domain defines ports (interfaces); adapters on the outside connect those ports to user interfaces, databases and other systems.
notes.extra: The domain depends on nothing external, so technology can be swapped and the domain tested in isolation. Cockburn (2005).
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 3: The Agile Architecture Capability

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::03 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Architecture Capability
notes.front: What is event-driven architecture?
notes.back: A style in which components communicate by publishing and reacting to events (facts that something happened) instead of calling each other directly. Producers do not know their consumers.
notes.extra: Gives loose coupling in time and in knowledge, at the cost of eventual consistency and harder tracing.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 3: The Agile Architecture Capability

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::03 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Architecture Capability
notes.front: What is event sourcing?
notes.back: Persisting the state of an entity as the ordered sequence of events that changed it, instead of storing only its current state. Current state is derived by replaying the events.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 3: The Agile Architecture Capability

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::03 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Architecture Capability
notes.front: What is Command Query Responsibility Segregation (CQRS)?
notes.back: Using separate models for changing state (commands) and for reading state (queries), so each side can be designed, scaled and stored independently.
notes.extra: Often paired with event sourcing: events from the write side feed the read models.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 3: The Agile Architecture Capability

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::03 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Architecture Capability
notes.front: What makes a service a microservice in the architectural sense?
notes.back: It is small enough for one team to own, encapsulates its own data, and is independently deployable. Ideally its boundary matches a bounded context of the domain.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 3: The Agile Architecture Capability

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::03 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Architecture Capability
notes.front: What is a saga, and what are its two coordination styles?
notes.back:
A sequence of local transactions across services, each with a compensating action to undo it, replacing a distributed transaction.
  • Orchestration: a central coordinator tells each participant what to do.
  • Choreography: participants react to each other's events with no central coordinator.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 3: The Agile Architecture Capability

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::03 Open Agile Architecture - The Agile Architecture Capability
notes.front: Why are DevOps and Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) practices treated as part of the architecture capability?
notes.back: The ability to change an architecture safely depends on how software is built, deployed and operated. Without fast, reliable delivery and operation, architectural refactoring is too slow and too risky.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 3: The Agile Architecture Capability

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::04 Open Agile Architecture - The Ways of Supporting
notes.front: Which techniques does Part 4 (The Ways of Supporting) cover in Version 2.0?
notes.back:
• experience design
  • journey mapping
  • Lean value stream mapping
  • event storming
  • Domain-Driven Design (DDD) patterns
  • data and Artificial Intelligence (AI) architectures
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 4: The Ways of Supporting

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::04 Open Agile Architecture - The Ways of Supporting
notes.front: What is design thinking, and what are its five modes?
notes.back:
A human-centred approach to framing and solving problems through iteration:
  1. Empathise
  2. Define
  3. Ideate
  4. Prototype
  5. Test
notes.extra: Stanford d.school formulation. The modes are revisited iteratively, not run once in sequence.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 4: The Ways of Supporting

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::04 Open Agile Architecture - The Ways of Supporting
notes.front: What is a persona?
notes.back: A fictional but research-based archetype representing a group of users with similar goals, behaviours and pain points, used to keep design decisions anchored on real needs.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 4: The Ways of Supporting

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::04 Open Agile Architecture - The Ways of Supporting
notes.front: What is a job-to-be-done?
notes.back: The progress a customer is trying to make in a given circumstance. Customers 'hire' a product to get that job done; the job, not the customer profile or the product, is the unit of analysis.
notes.extra: Jobs are stable over time while solutions change, which makes them a sound basis for segmentation and innovation.
notes.source: Christensen et al., Competing Against Luck (2016) · Open Agile Architecture / Part 4: The Ways of Supporting

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::04 Open Agile Architecture - The Ways of Supporting
notes.front: What is a customer journey map?
notes.back: A visualisation of the steps a customer goes through to reach a goal, with their actions, touchpoints, thoughts and emotions at each step, used to find pain points and opportunities.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 4: The Ways of Supporting

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::04 Open Agile Architecture - The Ways of Supporting
notes.front: What is a touchpoint?
notes.back: Any point of interaction between a customer and the enterprise (a website, app, call, shop, invoice, delivery) through which the experience is delivered.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 4: The Ways of Supporting

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::04 Open Agile Architecture - The Ways of Supporting
notes.front: What is an alignment diagram?
notes.back: Any map that puts the customer's experience and the organisation's activities side by side, to show where they do and do not line up.
notes.extra: Customer journey maps, service blueprints and experience maps are all alignment diagrams. Term from Kalbach, Mapping Experiences.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 4: The Ways of Supporting

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::04 Open Agile Architecture - The Ways of Supporting
notes.front: What does a service blueprint add to a customer journey map?
notes.back: The organisation's side of each step: front-stage actions, back-stage actions and support processes, separated by a line of interaction, a line of visibility and a line of internal interaction.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 4: The Ways of Supporting

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::04 Open Agile Architecture - The Ways of Supporting
notes.front: What does Lean value stream mapping show?
notes.back: The flow of material and information needed to deliver a product or service, step by step, with process time, waiting time and quality at each step, so that waste and bottlenecks become visible.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 4: The Ways of Supporting

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::04 Open Agile Architecture - The Ways of Supporting
notes.front: In value stream mapping, what is the difference between process time and lead time?
notes.back: Process time is the time work is actively being worked on. Lead time is the total elapsed time including waiting. The gap between them is delay.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 4: The Ways of Supporting

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::04 Open Agile Architecture - The Ways of Supporting
notes.front: What is Event Storming?
notes.back: A collaborative workshop in which business and technical people model a domain by placing domain events on a timeline with sticky notes, then adding commands, actors, policies and aggregates.
notes.extra: Invented by Alberto Brandolini. It surfaces boundaries, hot spots and shared language quickly.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 4: The Ways of Supporting

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::04 Open Agile Architecture - The Ways of Supporting
notes.front: What is a domain event?
notes.back: Something that happened in the domain that domain experts care about, named in the past tense (for example 'Order placed').
notes.extra: The orange sticky note in Event Storming.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 4: The Ways of Supporting

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::04 Open Agile Architecture - The Ways of Supporting
notes.text: Event Storming building blocks: a {{c1::command}} is a request that triggers an event; an {{c2::aggregate}} is the consistency boundary that handles commands and emits events; a {{c3::policy}} is a rule of the form 'whenever this event, then that command'; a {{c4::read model}} is the information an actor needs to make a decision.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 4: The Ways of Supporting

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::04 Open Agile Architecture - The Ways of Supporting
notes.front: What are the three levels at which Event Storming is run?
notes.back:
1. Big Picture: explore a whole business line to find boundaries and problems.
  2. Process Modelling: detail one process with commands, policies and read models.
  3. Software Design: derive aggregates and bounded contexts for implementation.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 4: The Ways of Supporting

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::04 Open Agile Architecture - The Ways of Supporting
notes.front: What is the ubiquitous language in Domain-Driven Design (DDD)?
notes.back: A shared, rigorous vocabulary built by domain experts and developers together, used consistently in conversation, models and code within one bounded context.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 4: The Ways of Supporting

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::04 Open Agile Architecture - The Ways of Supporting
notes.front: What is a bounded context?
notes.back: An explicit boundary within which a particular domain model and its language apply consistently. The same word may mean something different in another context.
notes.extra: Bounded contexts are the main candidate boundaries for teams and services.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 4: The Ways of Supporting

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::04 Open Agile Architecture - The Ways of Supporting
notes.text: Domain-Driven Design (DDD) classifies subdomains as {{c1::core}} (source of competitive advantage, build in-house), {{c2::supporting}} (necessary but not differentiating) and {{c3::generic}} (commodity, buy or reuse).
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 4: The Ways of Supporting

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::04 Open Agile Architecture - The Ways of Supporting
notes.front: What is a context map?
notes.back: A description of the bounded contexts in a system and the relationships between them, both technical (how models are translated) and organisational (which team depends on which).
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 4: The Ways of Supporting

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::04 Open Agile Architecture - The Ways of Supporting
notes.front: Name the main context-mapping relationship patterns of Domain-Driven Design (DDD).
notes.back:
• Partnership
  • Shared Kernel
  • Customer-Supplier
  • Conformist
  • Anticorruption Layer
  • Open Host Service
  • Published Language
  • Separate Ways
notes.source: Evans, Domain-Driven Design (2003) · Open Agile Architecture / Part 4: The Ways of Supporting

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::04 Open Agile Architecture - The Ways of Supporting
notes.front: What is an anticorruption layer?
notes.back: A translation layer a downstream context builds to isolate its own model from an upstream model it does not control, so foreign concepts do not leak into its domain.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 4: The Ways of Supporting

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::04 Open Agile Architecture - The Ways of Supporting
notes.front: Conformist versus Customer-Supplier: what distinguishes these context relationships?
notes.back: In Customer-Supplier the upstream team takes the downstream team's needs into its planning. In Conformist the upstream has no reason to accommodate, so the downstream simply adopts the upstream model.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 4: The Ways of Supporting

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::04 Open Agile Architecture - The Ways of Supporting
notes.front: What is an aggregate in Domain-Driven Design (DDD)?
notes.back: A cluster of domain objects treated as one unit for data changes, with a single root entity as the only entry point. Invariants are enforced inside it and it is a transactional consistency boundary.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 4: The Ways of Supporting

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::04 Open Agile Architecture - The Ways of Supporting
notes.front: What is a data mesh, and what are its four principles?
notes.back:
A decentralised approach to analytical data:
  1. domain-oriented ownership of data
  2. data as a product
  3. a self-serve data platform
  4. federated computational governance
notes.source: Dehghani, Data Mesh (2022) · Open Agile Architecture / Part 4: The Ways of Supporting

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::04 Open Agile Architecture - The Ways of Supporting
notes.front: What does it mean to treat data as a product?
notes.back: The team that owns a domain publishes its data for others with product qualities: discoverable, addressable, trustworthy, documented, interoperable and secure, with an accountable owner.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 4: The Ways of Supporting

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::04 Open Agile Architecture - The Ways of Supporting
notes.front: Why does a centralised, monolithic data platform conflict with Agile at scale?
notes.back: A central data team becomes a bottleneck between domain teams that produce data and those that consume it, and it lacks the domain knowledge to keep data meaningful as domains change.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group · Open Agile Architecture / Part 4: The Ways of Supporting

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::05 Open Agile Architecture - Axioms
notes.front: What are the axioms for the practice of Agile Architecture, and how many are there?
notes.back: 16 guiding principles that hold across contexts and anchor architecture decisions, covering customer experience, organisation, systems and change.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group, Appendix A · Open Agile Architecture / Axioms for the practice of Agile Architecture

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::05 Open Agile Architecture - Axioms
notes.front: List the 16 axioms for the practice of Agile Architecture.
notes.back:
1. Customer Experience Focus
  2. Outside-In Thinking
  3. Rapid Feedback Loops
  4. Touchpoint Orchestration
  5. Value Stream Alignment
  6. Autonomous Cross-Functional Teams
  7. Authority, Responsibility, and Accountability Distribution
  8. Loosely-Coupled Systems
  9. Modular Data Platform
  10. Simple Common Operating Principles
  11. Partitioning Over Layering
  12. Organization Mirroring Architecture
  13. Organizational Leveling
  14. Bias for Change
  15. Project to Product Shift
  16. Secure by Design
notes.extra: Grouping aid (mine, not part of the standard): 1-4 customer, 5-7 organisation, 8-11 systems, 12-13 organisation and architecture together, 14-16 change, lifecycle and security.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group, Appendix A · Open Agile Architecture / Axioms for the practice of Agile Architecture

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::05 Open Agile Architecture - Axioms
notes.front: Axiom: Customer Experience Focus. What does it ask for?
notes.back: Make the experience delivered to customers the starting point and the yardstick for product, operations and technology decisions.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group, Appendix A · Open Agile Architecture / Axioms for the practice of Agile Architecture

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::05 Open Agile Architecture - Axioms
notes.front: Axiom: Outside-In Thinking. What does it ask for?
notes.back: Start from customer problems and needs and work backwards to the solution and the capabilities required, instead of starting from existing internal capabilities and looking for uses.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group, Appendix A · Open Agile Architecture / Axioms for the practice of Agile Architecture

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::05 Open Agile Architecture - Axioms
notes.front: Axiom: Rapid Feedback Loops. What does it ask for?
notes.back: Collect feedback from customers and operations early and often, and feed it straight back into decisions, so wrong assumptions are found while they are still cheap to correct.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group, Appendix A · Open Agile Architecture / Axioms for the practice of Agile Architecture

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::05 Open Agile Architecture - Axioms
notes.front: Axiom: Touchpoint Orchestration. What does it ask for?
notes.back: Design and coordinate all customer touchpoints across channels as one coherent journey, instead of optimising each channel in its own silo.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group, Appendix A · Open Agile Architecture / Axioms for the practice of Agile Architecture

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::05 Open Agile Architecture - Axioms
notes.front: Axiom: Value Stream Alignment. What does it ask for?
notes.back: Organise teams and operations around the end-to-end streams that deliver value to customers, not around functions or technical specialisms.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group, Appendix A · Open Agile Architecture / Axioms for the practice of Agile Architecture

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::05 Open Agile Architecture - Axioms
notes.front: Axiom: Autonomous Cross-Functional Teams. What does it ask for?
notes.back: Small teams that hold all the skills needed to deliver their outcome and have the authority to decide how to do it, minimising hand-offs and dependencies.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group, Appendix A · Open Agile Architecture / Axioms for the practice of Agile Architecture

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::05 Open Agile Architecture - Axioms
notes.front: Axiom: Authority, Responsibility, and Accountability Distribution. What does it ask for?
notes.back: Push decision authority to the level where the relevant information is, and keep authority, responsibility and accountability matched: nobody is accountable for what they cannot decide.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group, Appendix A · Open Agile Architecture / Axioms for the practice of Agile Architecture

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::05 Open Agile Architecture - Axioms
notes.front: Axiom: Loosely-Coupled Systems. What does it ask for?
notes.back: Decompose systems into components with minimal, explicit dependencies, so each can be changed, deployed and scaled without coordinating with the others.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group, Appendix A · Open Agile Architecture / Axioms for the practice of Agile Architecture

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::05 Open Agile Architecture - Axioms
notes.front: Axiom: Modular Data Platform. What does it ask for?
notes.back: Partition data and its platform into loosely coupled, domain-owned parts instead of one central monolithic store, so data evolves at the pace of the domains.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group, Appendix A · Open Agile Architecture / Axioms for the practice of Agile Architecture

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::05 Open Agile Architecture - Axioms
notes.front: Axiom: Simple Common Operating Principles. What does it ask for?
notes.back: Coordinate autonomous teams through a small set of simple rules that everyone shares, instead of detailed central control.
notes.extra: Example: Amazon's rule that teams expose their data and functionality only through service interfaces.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group, Appendix A · Open Agile Architecture / Axioms for the practice of Agile Architecture

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::05 Open Agile Architecture - Axioms
notes.front: Axiom: Partitioning Over Layering. What does it ask for?
notes.back: Divide systems and teams along business or domain boundaries (vertical slices) in preference to horizontal technical layers, because layers force every change to cross several teams.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group, Appendix A · Open Agile Architecture / Axioms for the practice of Agile Architecture

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::05 Open Agile Architecture - Axioms
notes.front: Axiom: Organization Mirroring Architecture. What does it ask for?
notes.back: Shape the organisation to match the architecture you want, because system structure ends up copying the communication structure of the teams that build it.
notes.extra: Conway's Law used deliberately: the inverse Conway manoeuvre.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group, Appendix A · Open Agile Architecture / Axioms for the practice of Agile Architecture

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::05 Open Agile Architecture - Axioms
notes.front: Axiom: Organizational Leveling. What does it ask for?
notes.back: Recognise that the enterprise is structured in levels (enterprise, business unit, team of teams, team) and place each architectural concern and decision at the level able to resolve it.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group, Appendix A · Open Agile Architecture / Axioms for the practice of Agile Architecture

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::05 Open Agile Architecture - Axioms
notes.front: Axiom: Bias for Change. What does it ask for?
notes.back: Assume change is the normal state and design for it: prefer reversible decisions, evolvable structures and experiments over attempts to predict and lock in the future.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group, Appendix A · Open Agile Architecture / Axioms for the practice of Agile Architecture

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::05 Open Agile Architecture - Axioms
notes.front: Axiom: Project to Product Shift. What does it ask for?
notes.back: Replace temporary projects with long-lived product teams that own a product across its whole life, with persistent funding and accountability for outcomes rather than for delivering a scope.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group, Appendix A · Open Agile Architecture / Axioms for the practice of Agile Architecture

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::05 Open Agile Architecture - Axioms
notes.front: Axiom: Secure by Design. What does it ask for?
notes.back: Build security in from the first design decision and throughout the lifecycle, as a property of the architecture, instead of adding it through reviews at the end.
notes.source: Open Agile Architecture Standard, The Open Group, Appendix A · Open Agile Architecture / Axioms for the practice of Agile Architecture

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::06 Agile Foundations
notes.text: The Agile Manifesto was written in {{c1::February 2001}} at {{c2::Snowbird, Utah}} by {{c3::17}} software practitioners.
notes.extra: Among them Kent Beck, Ward Cunningham, Martin Fowler, Ken Schwaber, Jeff Sutherland and Alistair Cockburn.
notes.source: Manifesto for Agile Software Development (2001) · Agile foundations

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::06 Agile Foundations
notes.front: What are the four value statements of the Agile Manifesto?
notes.back:
• people and their interactions over processes and tools
  • working software over comprehensive documentation
  • collaboration with the customer over contract negotiation
  • responding to change over following a plan
notes.source: Manifesto for Agile Software Development (2001) · Agile foundations

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::06 Agile Foundations
notes.front: In the Agile Manifesto's value statements, what is the status of the right-hand items (processes, documentation, contracts, plans)?
notes.back: They still have value. The left-hand items are simply valued more when the two conflict.
notes.extra: The Manifesto does not say 'no documentation' or 'no plan'.
notes.source: Manifesto for Agile Software Development (2001) · Agile foundations

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::06 Agile Foundations
notes.front: According to the Agile principles, what is the primary measure of progress?
notes.back: Working software.
notes.extra: Not documents produced, tasks closed or hours spent.
notes.source: Manifesto for Agile Software Development (2001) · Agile foundations

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::06 Agile Foundations
notes.front: What delivery cadence do the Agile principles call for?
notes.back: Frequent delivery of working software, at intervals anywhere between two weeks and two months, the shorter the better.
notes.source: Manifesto for Agile Software Development (2001) · Agile foundations

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::06 Agile Foundations
notes.front: What do the Agile principles say about late requirement changes?
notes.back: They are to be welcomed, even late in development, because being able to absorb change gives the customer a competitive advantage.
notes.source: Manifesto for Agile Software Development (2001) · Agile foundations

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::06 Agile Foundations
notes.front: Which Agile principle addresses architecture directly?
notes.back: The one stating that self-organising teams are where the best architectures, requirements and designs come from.
notes.extra: A companion principle says that ongoing attention to technical excellence and good design increases agility.
notes.source: Manifesto for Agile Software Development (2001) · Agile foundations

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::06 Agile Foundations
notes.front: How do the Agile principles define simplicity?
notes.back: As maximising the amount of work that is not done. The principles call it an art, and essential.
notes.source: Manifesto for Agile Software Development (2001) · Agile foundations

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::06 Agile Foundations
notes.front: What do the Agile principles mean by sustainable development?
notes.back: Working at a pace that everyone involved (sponsors, developers, users) could keep up indefinitely. No heroics, no death marches.
notes.source: Manifesto for Agile Software Development (2001) · Agile foundations

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::06 Agile Foundations
notes.front: Iterative versus incremental development: what is the difference?
notes.back: Incremental: build the product piece by piece, each piece adding functionality. Iterative: revisit and refine the same thing in repeated passes based on feedback. Agile methods do both.
notes.source: Agile foundations

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::06 Agile Foundations
notes.front: What is empirical process control, and why does Agile rely on it?
notes.back: Controlling work through frequent inspection of real results and adaptation, instead of through a detailed predefined plan. It suits complex work, where the outcome cannot be predicted in advance.
notes.source: Agile foundations

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::06 Agile Foundations
notes.front: What did Winston Royce's 1970 paper, usually cited as the origin of 'waterfall', actually argue?
notes.back: That a strictly sequential process is risky and invites failure. He recommended iteration between phases and building the system twice.
notes.extra: He never used the word 'waterfall'.
notes.source: Royce, Managing the Development of Large Software Systems (1970) · Agile foundations

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::06 Agile Foundations
notes.front: Which 1986 article gave Scrum its name and core idea?
notes.back: 'The New New Product Development Game' by Takeuchi and Nonaka (Harvard Business Review): product development as a rugby-style team moving the ball together, instead of a relay race of hand-offs.
notes.source: Agile foundations

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::06 Agile Foundations
notes.text: The four steps of the Deming (Shewhart) improvement cycle are {{c1::Plan, Do, Check, Act}}.
notes.extra: Plan-Do-Check-Act (PDCA). Deming himself preferred 'Study' to 'Check'.
notes.source: Agile foundations

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::06 Agile Foundations
notes.text: John Boyd's decision loop has four steps: {{c1::Observe, Orient, Decide, Act}}.
notes.extra: The Observe-Orient-Decide-Act (OODA) loop. Whoever cycles through it faster than the competition gains the advantage.
notes.source: Agile foundations

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::06 Agile Foundations
notes.front: What are the domains of the Cynefin framework, and the fitting response in each?
notes.back:
• Clear: sense, categorise, respond (best practice)
  • Complicated: sense, analyse, respond (expertise, good practice)
  • Complex: probe, sense, respond (safe-to-fail experiments, emergent practice)
  • Chaotic: act, sense, respond (stabilise first)
  • Confusion: you do not yet know which domain applies
notes.extra: Agile methods are designed for the complex domain. Clear was formerly named Simple, later Obvious.
notes.source: Snowden and Boone, A Leader's Framework for Decision Making (2007) · Agile foundations

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::06 Agile Foundations
notes.front: What is a timebox?
notes.back: A fixed maximum duration for an activity. When time is up the activity ends and scope is what varies, not the deadline.
notes.source: Agile foundations

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::06 Agile Foundations
notes.front: What is business agility?
notes.back: The ability of a whole organisation, not only its software teams, to sense changes in its environment and respond quickly and effectively.
notes.source: Agile foundations

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::07 Scrum
notes.front: What is Scrum, in one sentence?
notes.back: A deliberately minimal framework for creating value on complex problems: a small team delivers in short cycles, inspecting results and adapting as it goes.
notes.extra: The 2020 edition is still the current official Scrum Guide.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (2020), Schwaber and Sutherland · Scrum

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::07 Scrum
notes.text: Scrum is founded on {{c1::empiricism}} and {{c2::lean thinking}}.
notes.extra: Empiricism: learn from experience and decide on observed evidence. Lean thinking: cut waste and keep to essentials.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (2020), Schwaber and Sutherland · Scrum

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::07 Scrum
notes.text: The three pillars of Scrum's empiricism are {{c1::transparency}}, {{c2::inspection}} and {{c3::adaptation}}.
notes.extra: Each depends on the one before: you cannot inspect what is not visible, and inspecting without adapting achieves nothing.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (2020), Schwaber and Sutherland · Scrum

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::07 Scrum
notes.text: The five Scrum values are {{c1::commitment, focus, openness, respect and courage}}.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (2020), Schwaber and Sutherland · Scrum

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::07 Scrum
notes.front: Which three accountabilities make up a Scrum Team?
notes.back:
• one Product Owner
  • one Scrum Master
  • Developers
notes.extra: Typically 10 or fewer people. No sub-teams and no hierarchy inside the team. The 2020 Guide speaks of accountabilities, not roles.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (2020), Schwaber and Sutherland · Scrum

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::07 Scrum
notes.front: What is the Product Owner accountable for?
notes.back: Getting the most value out of the product the Scrum Team builds, and managing the Product Backlog effectively.
notes.extra: One person, not a committee. Others may do backlog work, but accountability stays with the Product Owner.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (2020), Schwaber and Sutherland · Scrum

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::07 Scrum
notes.front: What is the Scrum Master accountable for?
notes.back: Making Scrum work as the Scrum Guide describes it, and the effectiveness of the Scrum Team.
notes.extra: Serves the team, the Product Owner and the organisation. Not a project manager.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (2020), Schwaber and Sutherland · Scrum

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::07 Scrum
notes.front: What are the Developers accountable for?
notes.back:
• planning the Sprint's work (the Sprint Backlog)
  • building quality in by meeting the Definition of Done
  • re-planning every day towards the Sprint Goal
  • holding one another to professional standards
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (2020), Schwaber and Sutherland · Scrum

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::07 Scrum
notes.text: The five Scrum events are the {{c1::Sprint}}, {{c2::Sprint Planning}}, {{c3::Daily Scrum}}, {{c4::Sprint Review}} and {{c5::Sprint Retrospective}}.
notes.extra: The Sprint is the container for the other four.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (2020), Schwaber and Sutherland · Scrum

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::07 Scrum
notes.text: A Sprint has a fixed length of {{c1::one month or less}}.
notes.extra: Shorter Sprints mean more frequent learning and less at stake in each one.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (2020), Schwaber and Sutherland · Scrum

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::07 Scrum
notes.front: Which three topics does Sprint Planning address?
notes.back:
1. Why: what makes this Sprint valuable (the Sprint Goal)
  2. What: which Product Backlog items can be completed
  3. How: how the selected work will be turned into an Increment
notes.extra: Goal, selected items and plan together form the Sprint Backlog.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (2020), Schwaber and Sutherland · Scrum

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::07 Scrum
notes.text: Scrum timeboxes for a one-month Sprint: Sprint Planning {{c1::8 hours}}, Daily Scrum {{c2::15 minutes}}, Sprint Review {{c3::4 hours}}, Sprint Retrospective {{c4::3 hours}}.
notes.extra: Maximums. Shorter Sprints usually have shorter events.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (2020), Schwaber and Sutherland · Scrum

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::07 Scrum
notes.front: What is the purpose of the Daily Scrum?
notes.back: The Developers check progress towards the Sprint Goal and re-plan the coming day's work, adjusting the Sprint Backlog as needed.
notes.extra: Not a status report to a manager. The 2020 Guide no longer prescribes the three questions.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (2020), Schwaber and Sutherland · Scrum

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::07 Scrum
notes.front: What is the purpose of the Sprint Review?
notes.back: The Scrum Team and stakeholders look at what the Sprint achieved and what has changed around it, and work out together what to do next. The Product Backlog may be adjusted.
notes.extra: A working session, not a presentation or sign-off gate.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (2020), Schwaber and Sutherland · Scrum

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::07 Scrum
notes.front: What is the purpose of the Sprint Retrospective?
notes.back: To find ways of working better: the team looks back at people, interactions, processes, tools and its Definition of Done, and picks the improvements with the most effect.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (2020), Schwaber and Sutherland · Scrum

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::07 Scrum
notes.text: Each Scrum artifact has a commitment: Product Backlog → {{c1::Product Goal}}; Sprint Backlog → {{c2::Sprint Goal}}; Increment → {{c3::Definition of Done}}.
notes.extra: Commitments were introduced in the 2020 Guide to increase transparency and focus.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (2020), Schwaber and Sutherland · Scrum

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::07 Scrum
notes.front: What is the Definition of Done?
notes.back: The team's explicit, shared quality bar: the conditions any work must meet before it counts as part of the Increment. Work that falls short is neither released nor shown at the Sprint Review; it goes back to the Product Backlog.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (2020), Schwaber and Sutherland · Scrum

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::07 Scrum
notes.front: What is an Increment in Scrum?
notes.back: A usable piece of product that moves towards the Product Goal. It adds to all earlier Increments, is verified to work together with them, and meets the Definition of Done.
notes.extra: Several Increments may be created in one Sprint. Release does not have to wait for the Sprint Review.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (2020), Schwaber and Sutherland · Scrum

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::07 Scrum
notes.front: Who can cancel a Sprint, and when?
notes.back: Only the Product Owner, when the Sprint Goal has become obsolete.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (2020), Schwaber and Sutherland · Scrum

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::07 Scrum
notes.front: What is Product Backlog refinement?
notes.back: The ongoing activity of breaking Product Backlog items down and adding detail (description, order, size) so they are ready for selection in Sprint Planning.
notes.extra: An activity, not one of the five events.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (2020), Schwaber and Sutherland · Scrum

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::07 Scrum
notes.front: Are velocity, story points, user stories and burndown charts part of Scrum?
notes.back: No. None of them appear in the Scrum Guide. They are complementary practices that many Scrum Teams choose to use.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (2020), Schwaber and Sutherland · Scrum

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::07 Scrum
notes.front: Can an organisation adopt only parts of Scrum and still call it Scrum?
notes.back: No. The framework is immutable: implementing only parts is possible, but the result is not Scrum. Scrum is a container for other practices, not a menu.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (2020), Schwaber and Sutherland · Scrum

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::08 Kanban and Flow
notes.front: What are the six general practices of the Kanban Method?
notes.back:
1. Visualise the work
  2. Limit Work In Progress (WIP)
  3. Manage flow
  4. Make policies explicit
  5. Implement feedback loops
  6. Improve collaboratively, evolve experimentally
notes.source: Anderson, Kanban (2010); Anderson and Carmichael, Essential Kanban Condensed (2016) · Kanban and flow

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::08 Kanban and Flow
notes.front: What are the three change-management principles of the Kanban Method?
notes.back:
1. Start with what you do now
  2. Agree to pursue improvement through evolutionary change
  3. Encourage acts of leadership at every level
notes.extra: Kanban is deliberately non-disruptive: it overlays the existing process instead of replacing it.
notes.source: Anderson, Kanban (2010); Anderson and Carmichael, Essential Kanban Condensed (2016) · Kanban and flow

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::08 Kanban and Flow
notes.front: Why limit Work In Progress (WIP)?
notes.back:
• turns a push system into a pull system
  • shortens cycle time
  • makes bottlenecks visible
  • reduces context switching
  • forces finishing before starting
notes.source: Kanban and flow

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::08 Kanban and Flow
notes.front: Push versus pull systems: what is the difference?
notes.back: In a push system work is assigned downstream regardless of capacity. In a pull system a step takes new work only when it has capacity, signalled by its Work In Progress (WIP) limit.
notes.source: Kanban and flow

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::08 Kanban and Flow
notes.text: The Kanban Guide's four mandatory flow measures are {{c1::Work In Progress (WIP)}}, {{c2::throughput}}, {{c3::work item age}} and {{c4::cycle time}}.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide, Vacanti and Coleman · Kanban and flow

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::08 Kanban and Flow
notes.text: Flow measures: {{c1::throughput}} is the number of items finished per unit of time; {{c2::cycle time}} is the elapsed time between an item starting and finishing; {{c3::work item age}} is the elapsed time since a still-unfinished item started.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide, Vacanti and Coleman · Kanban and flow

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::08 Kanban and Flow
notes.front: Lead time versus cycle time: what is the usual distinction?
notes.back: Lead time runs from the customer's request to delivery. Cycle time runs from when work actually starts to when it finishes. Lead time includes time waiting in the backlog.
notes.extra: Usage varies between sources; always state the start and end points you measure.
notes.source: Kanban and flow

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::08 Kanban and Flow
notes.front: State Little's Law as applied to a workflow.
notes.back: Average cycle time = average Work In Progress (WIP) ÷ average throughput.
notes.extra: Holds for a stable system. The practical reading: to shorten cycle time, lower WIP.
notes.source: Kanban and flow

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::08 Kanban and Flow
notes.front: What does a Cumulative Flow Diagram (CFD) show?
notes.back: The number of items in each workflow state over time, as stacked bands. The vertical distance between bands is Work In Progress (WIP); the horizontal distance approximates cycle time; a widening band signals a bottleneck.
notes.source: Kanban and flow

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::08 Kanban and Flow
notes.front: What is flow efficiency?
notes.back: Active working time ÷ total elapsed time for an item, as a percentage.
notes.extra: In knowledge work it is commonly very low, because items spend most of their time waiting in queues. Attack waiting time before working speed.
notes.source: Kanban and flow

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::08 Kanban and Flow
notes.front: What is a Service Level Expectation (SLE)?
notes.back: A statement of how long work items are expected to take from start to finish, given as an elapsed time plus a probability, for example '85% of items finish in 8 days or less'.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide, Vacanti and Coleman · Kanban and flow

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::08 Kanban and Flow
notes.text: Kanban's four classic classes of service are {{c1::expedite}}, {{c2::fixed date}}, {{c3::standard}} and {{c4::intangible}}.
notes.extra: Each class has its own cost-of-delay profile and therefore its own policy for selection and handling.
notes.source: Anderson, Kanban (2010); Anderson and Carmichael, Essential Kanban Condensed (2016) · Kanban and flow

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::08 Kanban and Flow
notes.front: What is Cost of Delay?
notes.back: The economic value lost per unit of time by delivering something later instead of now. It turns urgency into a number that can be compared with value and effort.
notes.source: Reinertsen, The Principles of Product Development Flow (2009) · Kanban and flow

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::08 Kanban and Flow
notes.front: What is Weighted Shortest Job First (WSJF)?
notes.back: A sequencing rule: do first the job with the highest Cost of Delay ÷ duration. It maximises economic benefit when jobs differ in both delay cost and size.
notes.extra: The Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe) approximates Cost of Delay as business value + time criticality + risk reduction or opportunity enablement.
notes.source: Reinertsen, The Principles of Product Development Flow (2009) · Kanban and flow

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::08 Kanban and Flow
notes.front: Why does reducing batch size improve flow?
notes.back:
• faster feedback
  • shorter cycle time
  • less variability
  • lower risk per release
  • less work stranded when priorities change
notes.extra: The optimum batch size balances holding cost against transaction cost; automation lowers transaction cost and so the optimum.
notes.source: Reinertsen, The Principles of Product Development Flow (2009) · Kanban and flow

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::08 Kanban and Flow
notes.front: Why are queues the central problem in product development, according to Reinertsen?
notes.back: Queues of invisible work in progress lengthen cycle time, delay feedback, raise risk and variability, and lower quality and motivation, yet they are rarely measured.
notes.extra: High capacity utilisation makes queues grow non-linearly.
notes.source: Reinertsen, The Principles of Product Development Flow (2009) · Kanban and flow

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::08 Kanban and Flow
notes.front: What are the five focusing steps of the Theory of Constraints?
notes.back:
1. Identify the constraint
  2. Exploit it (get the most from it as it is)
  3. Subordinate everything else to it
  4. Elevate it (add capacity)
  5. Repeat: do not let inertia become the constraint
notes.extra: Any improvement made away from the constraint is an illusion.
notes.source: Goldratt, The Goal (1984) · Kanban and flow

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::08 Kanban and Flow
notes.front: Why is probabilistic forecasting preferred over single-date estimates in flow-based planning?
notes.back: Delivery times vary. A forecast drawn from historical throughput or cycle-time data (for example by Monte Carlo simulation) gives a date range with a confidence level, which is honest about uncertainty.
notes.source: Kanban and flow

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::09 Lean
notes.text: The two pillars of the Toyota Production System are {{c1::Just-in-Time}} and {{c2::Jidoka}}.
notes.source: Ohno, Toyota Production System (1988) · Lean

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::09 Lean
notes.front: What is Just-in-Time?
notes.back: Producing only what is needed, when it is needed, in the amount needed, so that inventory and waiting are minimised and problems surface quickly.
notes.source: Ohno, Toyota Production System (1988) · Lean

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::09 Lean
notes.front: What is Jidoka?
notes.back: Automation with a human touch: equipment and people detect abnormalities and stop immediately, so defects are never passed downstream and the cause can be fixed at once.
notes.extra: Software analogue: a failing build stops the pipeline.
notes.source: Ohno, Toyota Production System (1988) · Lean

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::09 Lean
notes.front: What are the seven wastes identified by Taiichi Ohno?
notes.back:
• Transportation
  • Inventory
  • Motion
  • Waiting
  • Overproduction
  • Overprocessing
  • Defects
notes.extra: Mnemonic: TIMWOOD. Ohno considered overproduction the worst because it hides the others.
notes.source: Ohno, Toyota Production System (1988) · Lean

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::09 Lean
notes.front: What are the seven wastes of software development, per Mary and Tom Poppendieck?
notes.back:
• partially done work
  • extra features
  • relearning
  • hand-offs
  • task switching
  • delays
  • defects
notes.source: Poppendieck and Poppendieck, Implementing Lean Software Development (2006) · Lean

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::09 Lean
notes.text: Lean's three kinds of loss: {{c1::Muda}} is waste, {{c2::Mura}} is unevenness and {{c3::Muri}} is overburden.
notes.extra: Unevenness and overburden usually cause the waste; removing waste alone does not last.
notes.source: Lean

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::09 Lean
notes.front: What are the five principles of Lean Thinking?
notes.back:
1. Specify value from the customer's standpoint
  2. Identify the value stream
  3. Make value flow
  4. Let the customer pull
  5. Pursue perfection
notes.source: Womack and Jones, Lean Thinking (1996) · Lean

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::09 Lean
notes.front: What are the seven principles of Lean Software Development (2006 formulation)?
notes.back:
1. Eliminate waste
  2. Build quality in
  3. Create knowledge
  4. Defer commitment
  5. Deliver fast
  6. Respect people
  7. Optimise the whole
notes.source: Poppendieck and Poppendieck, Implementing Lean Software Development (2006) · Lean

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::09 Lean
notes.front: What is Kaizen?
notes.back: Continuous improvement in small steps, carried out by the people who do the work, as part of the daily job.
notes.source: Lean

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::09 Lean
notes.front: What is the Gemba, and what is a Gemba walk?
notes.back: The place where the work actually happens. A Gemba walk means going there to observe and ask questions, instead of managing from reports.
notes.source: Lean

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::09 Lean
notes.front: What is an Andon?
notes.back: A signal (originally a cord and a light board) with which any worker flags a problem and can stop the line, so that help arrives and the problem is solved where it occurs.
notes.source: Lean

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::09 Lean
notes.front: What is Poka-yoke?
