notes.back: Mistake-proofing: designing a process or device so an error is impossible or immediately obvious.
notes.extra: Software analogues: type systems, schema validation, a pipeline that refuses unsigned artefacts.
notes.source: Lean

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::09 Lean
notes.front: What is takt time?
notes.back: Available working time ÷ customer demand in that period: the pace at which units must be completed to meet demand exactly.
notes.source: Lean

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::09 Lean
notes.front: What is the Five Whys technique?
notes.back: Asking 'why?' repeatedly (about five times) about a problem to move from the symptom to a root cause that can be fixed.
notes.extra: Weakness: it tends to follow a single causal chain; complex failures usually have several contributing causes.
notes.source: Lean

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::09 Lean
notes.front: What is the Build-Measure-Learn loop?
notes.back: The Lean Startup feedback cycle: turn an idea into the smallest product that tests it, measure how customers respond, and learn whether to persevere or pivot. Total time through the loop is what to minimise.
notes.source: Ries, The Lean Startup (2011) · Lean

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::09 Lean
notes.front: What is a Minimum Viable Product (MVP)?
notes.back: The smallest thing you can build that lets you test a hypothesis about customers and learn from their real behaviour.
notes.extra: A learning tool, not a cut-down first release.
notes.source: Ries, The Lean Startup (2011) · Lean

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::09 Lean
notes.front: What is a pivot in the Lean Startup?
notes.back: A deliberate change of direction, based on what was learned, to try a different core assumption about the product or its market, without discarding the learning so far.
notes.source: Ries, The Lean Startup (2011) · Lean

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::10 Extreme Programming and Engineering Practices
notes.text: The five values of Extreme Programming (XP) are {{c1::communication, simplicity, feedback, courage and respect}}.
notes.source: Beck, Extreme Programming Explained (2nd ed., 2004) · Extreme Programming and engineering practices

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::10 Extreme Programming and Engineering Practices
notes.front: What is the cycle of Test-Driven Development (TDD)?
notes.back:
1. Red: write a small failing test
  2. Green: write the simplest code that passes it
  3. Refactor: clean up while the tests stay green
notes.extra: The tests drive the design, and form a regression net that makes later refactoring safe.
notes.source: Beck, Test-Driven Development: By Example (2002) · Extreme Programming and engineering practices

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::10 Extreme Programming and Engineering Practices
notes.front: What is pair programming?
notes.back: Two developers working on the same code at one workstation: the driver writes, the navigator reviews and thinks ahead, and they swap often.
notes.extra: Continuous review and knowledge sharing in exchange for short-term capacity.
notes.source: Beck, Extreme Programming Explained (2nd ed., 2004) · Extreme Programming and engineering practices

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::10 Extreme Programming and Engineering Practices
notes.front: What is Continuous Integration?
notes.back: Every developer merges into the shared mainline at least daily, and each merge is verified by an automated build and test run. A broken build is fixed immediately.
notes.extra: It is a practice, not a tool: running a build server on long-lived branches is not Continuous Integration.
notes.source: Fowler, Continuous Integration (2006) · Extreme Programming and engineering practices

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::10 Extreme Programming and Engineering Practices
notes.front: What are Kent Beck's four rules of simple design, in priority order?
notes.back:
1. Passes the tests
  2. Reveals intention
  3. No duplication
  4. Fewest elements
notes.source: Extreme Programming and engineering practices

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::10 Extreme Programming and Engineering Practices
notes.front: What does YAGNI stand for, and what does it advise?
notes.back: You Aren't Gonna Need It (YAGNI): do not build a capability until it is actually needed, because speculative features cost effort to build, carry and work around, and are often wrong.
notes.source: Extreme Programming and engineering practices

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::10 Extreme Programming and Engineering Practices
notes.front: What is collective code ownership?
notes.back: Anyone on the team may improve any part of the code at any time. It removes bottlenecks around individuals and depends on shared standards and a strong test suite.
notes.source: Beck, Extreme Programming Explained (2nd ed., 2004) · Extreme Programming and engineering practices

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::10 Extreme Programming and Engineering Practices
notes.front: What are the three Cs of a user story?
notes.back:
• Card: a short written token of the story
  • Conversation: the discussion that fills in the detail
  • Confirmation: the acceptance tests that show it is done
notes.extra: A story is a placeholder for a conversation, not a specification.
notes.source: Jeffries (2001) · Extreme Programming and engineering practices

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::10 Extreme Programming and Engineering Practices
notes.front: What does the INVEST checklist say a good user story is?
notes.back:
• Independent
  • Negotiable
  • Valuable
  • Estimable
  • Small
  • Testable
notes.source: Wake (2003) · Extreme Programming and engineering practices

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::10 Extreme Programming and Engineering Practices
notes.front: What is the Given-When-Then format?
notes.back: A structure for acceptance criteria from Behaviour-Driven Development (BDD): Given a context, When an event occurs, Then an observable outcome follows.
notes.extra: Each scenario is a concrete example that can be automated as a test.
notes.source: Extreme Programming and engineering practices

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::10 Extreme Programming and Engineering Practices
notes.front: What is a spike?
notes.back: A short, timeboxed investigation or throwaway experiment to reduce uncertainty about a technical approach or a requirement before committing to it.
notes.source: Extreme Programming and engineering practices

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::10 Extreme Programming and Engineering Practices
notes.front: What are the two axes of Martin Fowler's technical debt quadrant?
notes.back: Reckless or prudent, and deliberate or inadvertent.
notes.extra:
• Prudent and deliberate: a known shortcut taken consciously, with a plan to repay
  • Reckless and deliberate: knowingly skipping design for lack of time
  • Reckless and inadvertent: not knowing good design practice
  • Prudent and inadvertent: learning only in hindsight what the design should have been
notes.source: Fowler, Technical Debt Quadrant (2009) · Extreme Programming and engineering practices

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::10 Extreme Programming and Engineering Practices
notes.front: What is trunk-based development?
notes.back: All developers integrate small changes into a single shared branch at least daily; branches, if used, live for hours, not weeks. Unfinished work is hidden behind feature toggles.
notes.extra: A prerequisite for real Continuous Integration.
notes.source: Extreme Programming and engineering practices

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::10 Extreme Programming and Engineering Practices
notes.front: What is a feature toggle?
notes.back: A runtime switch that turns a code path on or off without redeploying. It separates deploying code from releasing a feature.
notes.extra: Toggles are inventory: remove them once the feature is fully released.
notes.source: Extreme Programming and engineering practices

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::10 Extreme Programming and Engineering Practices
notes.front: What does the test pyramid recommend?
notes.back: Many fast unit tests at the base, fewer service or integration tests in the middle, and very few slow end-to-end tests through the User Interface (UI) at the top.
notes.source: Cohn, Succeeding with Agile (2009) · Extreme Programming and engineering practices

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::11 DevOps and Delivery Performance
notes.front: What are the Three Ways of DevOps?
notes.back:
1. Flow: fast left-to-right flow of work from development to operations to the customer
  2. Feedback: fast, constant feedback from right to left at every stage
  3. Continual learning and experimentation: a high-trust culture that takes risks and learns from failure
notes.source: Kim, Humble, Debois, Willis, The DevOps Handbook (2nd ed., 2021) · DevOps and delivery performance

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::11 DevOps and Delivery Performance
notes.text: The CALMS model of DevOps stands for {{c1::Culture, Automation, Lean, Measurement, Sharing}}.
notes.source: DevOps and delivery performance

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::11 DevOps and Delivery Performance
notes.front: DevOps Research and Assessment (DORA) measures software delivery performance with five metrics. Which three measure throughput?
notes.back:
• Change lead time: from commit to running in production
  • Deployment frequency: how often changes are deployed to production
  • Failed deployment recovery time: how long it takes to recover from a deployment that failed
notes.extra: Recovery time was counted under stability in the original 'four keys' as time to restore service.
notes.source: DevOps Research and Assessment (DORA), dora.dev · DevOps and delivery performance

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::11 DevOps and Delivery Performance
notes.front: DevOps Research and Assessment (DORA) measures software delivery performance with five metrics. Which two measure instability?
notes.back:
• Change fail rate: share of deployments that need immediate intervention
  • Deployment rework rate: share of deployments that are unplanned and made to fix a production problem
notes.extra: Rework rate is the fifth metric, added to the original four keys.
notes.source: DevOps Research and Assessment (DORA), dora.dev · DevOps and delivery performance

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::11 DevOps and Delivery Performance
notes.front: What is the central finding of the DevOps Research and Assessment (DORA) research about speed and stability?
notes.back: They are not a trade-off. Teams that deliver faster also tend to be more stable, because both come from the same capabilities: small batches, automation, fast feedback.
notes.source: Forsgren, Humble, Kim, Accelerate (2018) · DevOps and delivery performance

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::11 DevOps and Delivery Performance
notes.front: Continuous Delivery versus Continuous Deployment: what is the difference?
notes.back: Continuous Delivery: every change that passes the pipeline is releasable, and releasing is a business decision made at the push of a button. Continuous Deployment: every change that passes is released to production automatically.
notes.source: Humble and Farley, Continuous Delivery (2010) · DevOps and delivery performance

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::11 DevOps and Delivery Performance
notes.front: What is a deployment pipeline?
notes.back: The automated path every change takes from commit to production: build, automated tests of increasing scope, and deployment through environments. It is the only route to production.
notes.source: Humble and Farley, Continuous Delivery (2010) · DevOps and delivery performance

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::11 DevOps and Delivery Performance
notes.front: Why separate deployment from release?
notes.back: Deployment (putting code into production) is a technical event; release (exposing a feature to users) is a business decision. Separating them makes deployments small, frequent and low-risk.
notes.source: DevOps and delivery performance

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::11 DevOps and Delivery Performance
notes.front: What is a blue-green deployment?
notes.back: Two identical production environments: the new version is deployed to the idle one, verified, and traffic is switched over. Rollback is switching back.
notes.source: DevOps and delivery performance

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::11 DevOps and Delivery Performance
notes.front: What is a canary release?
notes.back: Rolling a new version out to a small share of users or servers first, watching its metrics, and widening the rollout only if it behaves well.
notes.source: DevOps and delivery performance

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::11 DevOps and Delivery Performance
notes.front: What is Infrastructure as Code?
notes.back: Defining infrastructure in version-controlled, machine-readable files and provisioning it through automation, so environments are reproducible, reviewable and testable.
notes.source: DevOps and delivery performance

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::11 DevOps and Delivery Performance
notes.front: What does shift left mean?
notes.back: Moving testing, security and quality checks earlier in the delivery process, where problems are cheaper to find and fix.
notes.source: DevOps and delivery performance

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::11 DevOps and Delivery Performance
notes.text: In Site Reliability Engineering (SRE): a {{c1::Service Level Indicator (SLI)}} is a measured aspect of service behaviour; a {{c2::Service Level Objective (SLO)}} is the target value for it; a {{c3::Service Level Agreement (SLA)}} is a contract with consequences if the target is missed.
notes.source: Beyer et al., Site Reliability Engineering (Google, 2016) · DevOps and delivery performance

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::11 DevOps and Delivery Performance
notes.front: What is an error budget?
notes.back: The amount of unreliability a service is allowed: 100% minus its Service Level Objective (SLO). While budget remains, teams may ship; once it is spent, effort shifts to reliability.
notes.extra: It turns the conflict between development speed and operational stability into a shared, measurable rule.
notes.source: Beyer et al., Site Reliability Engineering (Google, 2016) · DevOps and delivery performance

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::11 DevOps and Delivery Performance
notes.front: What is toil in Site Reliability Engineering (SRE)?
notes.back: Operational work that is manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical, without lasting value, and that grows in proportion to the service.
notes.extra: Google aims to keep it below half of an engineer's time.
notes.source: Beyer et al., Site Reliability Engineering (Google, 2016) · DevOps and delivery performance

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::11 DevOps and Delivery Performance
notes.front: What makes a postmortem blameless?
notes.back: It assumes people acted reasonably on the information they had, and looks for the systemic conditions that made the failure possible, so people report problems openly instead of hiding them.
notes.source: Beyer et al., Site Reliability Engineering (Google, 2016) · DevOps and delivery performance

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::11 DevOps and Delivery Performance
notes.front: What are the three culture types in Westrum's typology?
notes.back:
• Pathological: power-oriented; information is hoarded, messengers are punished
  • Bureaucratic: rule-oriented; information follows channels, messengers are ignored
  • Generative: performance-oriented; information flows freely, messengers are trained
notes.extra: Generative culture predicts software delivery and organisational performance in the DevOps Research and Assessment (DORA) research.
notes.source: Westrum, A Typology of Organisational Cultures (2004) · DevOps and delivery performance

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::11 DevOps and Delivery Performance
notes.front: What does 'you build it, you run it' mean?
notes.back: The team that develops a service also operates it in production, so it feels the consequences of its design decisions and has direct contact with users.
notes.extra: Werner Vogels, Amazon (2006).
notes.source: DevOps and delivery performance

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::11 DevOps and Delivery Performance
notes.front: What is an internal developer platform?
notes.back: A self-service layer of tools, services and paved paths, built and run as a product by a platform team, that lets delivery teams build, deploy and operate software without needing specialists for each step.
notes.source: DevOps and delivery performance

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::12 Teams and Organisation
notes.front: State Conway's Law.
notes.back: Organisations design systems whose structure copies the organisation's own communication structure.
notes.source: Conway, How Do Committees Invent? (1968) · Teams and organisation

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::12 Teams and Organisation
notes.front: What is the inverse Conway manoeuvre?
notes.back: Deliberately shaping team structure and communication paths to match the architecture you want, so that Conway's Law works for you instead of against you.
notes.source: Teams and organisation

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::12 Teams and Organisation
notes.text: Team Topologies defines four team types: {{c1::stream-aligned}}, {{c2::enabling}}, {{c3::complicated-subsystem}} and {{c4::platform}}.
notes.extra: Stream-aligned is the primary type; the other three exist to reduce its load.
notes.source: Skelton and Pais, Team Topologies (2019) · Teams and organisation

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::12 Teams and Organisation
notes.text: Team Topologies defines three team interaction modes: {{c1::collaboration}}, {{c2::X-as-a-Service}} and {{c3::facilitating}}.
notes.source: Skelton and Pais, Team Topologies (2019) · Teams and organisation

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::12 Teams and Organisation
notes.front: In Team Topologies, when is the collaboration interaction mode appropriate, and what does it cost?
notes.back: For discovery: when two teams need to explore something new together for a limited time. It costs cognitive load and blurs responsibility, so it should not be permanent.
notes.source: Skelton and Pais, Team Topologies (2019) · Teams and organisation

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::12 Teams and Organisation
notes.front: In Team Topologies, what is an enabling team?
notes.back: A team of specialists that helps stream-aligned teams acquire a missing capability, then steps away. It teaches; it does not do the work for them.
notes.source: Skelton and Pais, Team Topologies (2019) · Teams and organisation

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::12 Teams and Organisation
notes.front: In Team Topologies, what is a complicated-subsystem team?
notes.back: A team that owns a part of the system needing deep specialist knowledge (for example a pricing engine or a video codec), so stream-aligned teams do not each have to master it.
notes.source: Skelton and Pais, Team Topologies (2019) · Teams and organisation

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::12 Teams and Organisation
notes.front: Why does Team Topologies treat team cognitive load as the main design constraint?
notes.back: A team can only own as much software as it can understand and operate well. Exceed that and delivery slows, quality drops and ownership dissolves. Boundaries are sized to the team, not the other way round.
notes.source: Skelton and Pais, Team Topologies (2019) · Teams and organisation

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::12 Teams and Organisation
notes.text: Cognitive load theory distinguishes three kinds of load: {{c1::intrinsic}} (inherent difficulty of the task), {{c2::extraneous}} (caused by the environment and how the task is presented) and {{c3::germane}} (effort that builds learning).
notes.extra: Team design aim: minimise extraneous load, keep intrinsic load manageable, leave room for germane load.
notes.source: Sweller, van Merrienboer, Paas, cognitive load theory (1998) · Teams and organisation

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::12 Teams and Organisation
notes.front: What is a Thinnest Viable Platform?
notes.back: The smallest set of interfaces, documentation and services that speeds up stream-aligned teams. It may be as little as a wiki page describing how to use underlying services.
notes.source: Skelton and Pais, Team Topologies (2019) · Teams and organisation

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::12 Teams and Organisation
notes.front: What is a team Application Programming Interface (API)?
notes.back: Everything through which other teams interact with a team: its code and service interfaces, documentation, working practices, communication channels and roadmap.
notes.source: Skelton and Pais, Team Topologies (2019) · Teams and organisation

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::12 Teams and Organisation
notes.front: State Brooks's Law.
notes.back: Adding people to a late software project delays it further: new people need ramp-up time and the number of communication paths grows with the square of team size.
notes.source: Brooks, The Mythical Man-Month (1975) · Teams and organisation

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::12 Teams and Organisation
notes.text: Tuckman's stages of group development are {{c1::forming, storming, norming and performing}}.
notes.extra: A fifth stage, adjourning, was added in 1977. Changing team membership sends a team back to earlier stages, which is an argument for long-lived teams.
notes.source: Teams and organisation

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::12 Teams and Organisation
notes.front: What is psychological safety?
notes.back: The climate in a team where members trust that speaking up will not be held against them: they can ask questions, admit mistakes and disagree without fear of punishment or humiliation.
notes.extra: Google's Project Aristotle found it the strongest predictor of team effectiveness.
notes.source: Edmondson (1999) · Teams and organisation

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::12 Teams and Organisation
notes.front: What is Dunbar's number, and why does it matter for organisation design?
notes.back: Roughly 150: the suggested upper limit on stable social relationships one person can maintain. Smaller thresholds (about 5, 15, 50) bound close trust, which is why teams stay small and groups of teams are capped.
notes.source: Teams and organisation

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::12 Teams and Organisation
notes.front: What is a two-pizza team?
notes.back: Amazon's rule of thumb that a team should be small enough to be fed by two pizzas (under about ten people), owning a service end to end with a single-threaded focus.
notes.source: Teams and organisation

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::12 Teams and Organisation
notes.text: In the Spotify model, a {{c1::squad}} is a small autonomous cross-functional team; a {{c2::tribe}} groups squads working in a related area; a {{c3::chapter}} groups people of one discipline within a tribe; a {{c4::guild}} is a voluntary community of interest across the company.
notes.extra: It described Spotify in 2012, not a framework. Its authors warned against copying it.
notes.source: Kniberg and Ivarsson, Scaling Agile @ Spotify (2012) · Teams and organisation

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::12 Teams and Organisation
notes.front: State Goodhart's Law and its consequence for Agile metrics.
notes.back: When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. Targets on velocity, story points or utilisation get gamed; measure outcomes and flow, and use metrics for learning, not for judging people.
notes.source: Teams and organisation

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::12 Teams and Organisation
notes.front: What are T-shaped skills?
notes.back: Deep expertise in one area (the vertical bar) combined with enough breadth to collaborate and help in adjacent areas (the horizontal bar). They make cross-functional teams resilient to bottlenecks.
notes.source: Teams and organisation

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::13 Scaling Frameworks
notes.front: What should be tried before adopting a scaling framework?
notes.back: Descaling: reduce the need for coordination by cutting dependencies, through modular architecture, clearer product boundaries and cross-functional teams. Frameworks manage dependencies; they do not remove them.
notes.source: Scaling frameworks

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::13 Scaling Frameworks
notes.front: In the Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe), what is an Agile Release Train (ART)?
notes.back: A long-lived team of Agile teams (about 50 to 125 people) that plans, commits and delivers together on a shared cadence, aligned to a value stream.
notes.source: Scaled Agile Framework, scaledagileframework.com · Scaling frameworks

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::13 Scaling Frameworks
notes.front: In the Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe), what are a Planning Interval (PI) and PI Planning?
notes.back: A Planning Interval is a timebox of typically 8 to 12 weeks. PI Planning is the event in which all teams of an Agile Release Train plan the interval together, agree objectives and expose dependencies.
notes.extra: Before SAFe 6.0 the abbreviation stood for Program Increment.
notes.source: Scaled Agile Framework, scaledagileframework.com · Scaling frameworks

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::13 Scaling Frameworks
notes.front: In the Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe), what is an enabler?
notes.back: A backlog item for work that does not deliver user value directly but makes future delivery possible: exploration, architecture, infrastructure or compliance. Enablers extend the architectural runway.
notes.source: Scaled Agile Framework, scaledagileframework.com · Scaling frameworks

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::13 Scaling Frameworks
notes.front: What defines Large-Scale Scrum (LeSS)?
notes.back: Scrum applied to several teams working on one product, with one Product Owner, one Product Backlog, one Definition of Done and one shared Sprint. Up to about eight teams; beyond that, LeSS Huge.
notes.extra: Its stance: scale by removing organisational complexity, not by adding roles and processes.
notes.source: Larman and Vodde, Large-Scale Scrum (2016) · Scaling frameworks

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::13 Scaling Frameworks
notes.front: What is Nexus?
notes.back: A scaling framework from Scrum.org for roughly three to nine Scrum Teams building one product from one Product Backlog. It adds a Nexus Integration Team accountable for producing an integrated Increment each Sprint.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (2021) · Scaling frameworks

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::13 Scaling Frameworks
notes.front: What is a Scrum of Scrums?
notes.back: A coordination meeting in which representatives of several teams synchronise on cross-team dependencies, integration and impediments.
notes.source: Scaling frameworks

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::13 Scaling Frameworks
notes.front: What is Disciplined Agile?
notes.back: A toolkit from the Project Management Institute (PMI) that, instead of prescribing one process, offers context-dependent options and guides teams in choosing their own way of working.
notes.source: Scaling frameworks

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::13 Scaling Frameworks
notes.front: What is the most common criticism of heavyweight scaling frameworks?
notes.back: They add roles, layers and synchronised planning that can recreate central control and plan-driven delivery under Agile vocabulary, while leaving the underlying coupling in architecture and organisation untouched.
notes.source: Scaling frameworks

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::14 Product and Discovery
notes.front: Output, outcome, impact: what does each measure?
notes.back:
• Output: what was produced (features, releases)
  • Outcome: the change in customer or user behaviour it caused
  • Impact: the resulting effect on the business
notes.source: Seiden, Outcomes Over Output (2019) · Product and discovery

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::14 Product and Discovery
notes.front: Product discovery versus product delivery: what is each for?
notes.back: Discovery decides what is worth building, by testing ideas quickly and cheaply. Delivery builds and ships it to production quality. They run continuously and in parallel.
notes.source: Cagan, Inspired (2nd ed., 2017) · Product and discovery

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::14 Product and Discovery
notes.text: Marty Cagan's four product risks are {{c1::value}} (will customers buy or use it?), {{c2::usability}} (can they work out how to use it?), {{c3::feasibility}} (can we build it?) and {{c4::business viability}} (does it work for our business?).
notes.extra: Discovery exists to address these before delivery, not after.
notes.source: Cagan, Inspired (2nd ed., 2017) · Product and discovery

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::14 Product and Discovery
notes.front: How does a product operating model differ from a project one?
notes.back:
• long-lived teams instead of temporary ones
  • funding of teams and outcomes instead of scopes
  • success measured by outcomes instead of on time and on budget
  • the team that builds also maintains and improves
  • work is brought to the team, not people to the work
notes.source: Product and discovery

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::14 Product and Discovery
notes.front: What is a user story map?
notes.back: A two-dimensional arrangement of user stories: the horizontal axis follows the user's activities in order (the backbone); the vertical axis orders the stories under each activity by priority. Horizontal slices become releases.
notes.source: Patton, User Story Mapping (2014) · Product and discovery

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::14 Product and Discovery
notes.text: An impact map answers four questions in order: {{c1::Why}} (the goal), {{c2::Who}} (the actors), {{c3::How}} (the behaviour changes wanted from them) and {{c4::What}} (the deliverables).
notes.source: Adzic, Impact Mapping (2012) · Product and discovery

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::14 Product and Discovery
notes.front: What is an Opportunity Solution Tree?
notes.back: A visual that links a desired outcome at the root to the customer opportunities (needs, pains, desires) that could drive it, then to candidate solutions, then to the experiments that test their assumptions.
notes.source: Torres, Continuous Discovery Habits (2021) · Product and discovery

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::14 Product and Discovery
notes.front: What are the three main feature categories of the Kano model?
notes.back:
• Must-be: expected; absence causes dissatisfaction, presence goes unnoticed
  • Performance: the more, the more satisfaction
  • Attractive: unexpected delighters; absence does not hurt
notes.extra: Over time delighters decay into must-bes.
notes.source: Product and discovery

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::14 Product and Discovery
notes.text: MoSCoW prioritisation sorts requirements into {{c1::Must have, Should have, Could have and Won't have (this time)}}.
notes.extra: From the Dynamic Systems Development Method (DSDM).
notes.source: Product and discovery

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::14 Product and Discovery
notes.front: What are story points, and what are they not?
notes.back: A relative, unitless estimate of a backlog item's size combining effort, complexity and uncertainty. They are not hours, not comparable between teams, and not a measure of productivity.
notes.source: Product and discovery

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::14 Product and Discovery
notes.front: What is velocity, and what is it legitimately used for?
notes.back: The amount of work (often in story points) a team completes per iteration. It is a planning aid for that team's own forecasting, not a performance target and not comparable between teams.
notes.source: Product and discovery

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::14 Product and Discovery
notes.front: What is dual-track Agile?
notes.back: Running discovery and delivery as two continuous, parallel tracks within the same team: discovery produces validated backlog items, delivery turns them into shipped software.
notes.source: Product and discovery

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::14 Product and Discovery
notes.front: How is a product hypothesis usually written?
notes.back: 'We believe that [this change] for [these users] will result in [this outcome]. We will know we are right when we see [this measurable signal].'
notes.source: Product and discovery

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::14 Product and Discovery
notes.front: What is the structure of a now-next-later roadmap?
notes.back: Three horizons with decreasing certainty and detail: now (in progress, well defined), next (committed direction, less detail), later (options and themes). It avoids dates that imply false precision.
notes.source: Product and discovery

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::15 Evolutionary Architecture
notes.front: What is an evolutionary architecture?
notes.back: An architecture built to keep changing in small, controlled steps along several dimensions at once (technical, data, security, operational), with fitness functions steering each change.
notes.source: Ford, Parsons, Kua, Building Evolutionary Architectures (2017) · Evolutionary architecture

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::15 Evolutionary Architecture
notes.front: Give a pragmatic definition of software architecture useful in Agile contexts.
notes.back: The set of design decisions that are hard to change later and that the team needs to get right early; the shared understanding of how the system is put together.
notes.source: Fowler, Who Needs an Architect? (2003) · Evolutionary architecture

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::15 Evolutionary Architecture
notes.front: What is an Architecture Decision Record (ADR)?
notes.back: A short document capturing one architecturally significant decision: its context, the decision itself, its status and its consequences. Records are kept with the code and never rewritten, only superseded.
notes.source: Nygard, Documenting Architecture Decisions (2011) · Evolutionary architecture

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::15 Evolutionary Architecture
notes.front: What is the last responsible moment?
notes.back: The latest point at which a decision can still be made without a valuable alternative being closed off by default. Deciding then means deciding with the most information available.
notes.source: Poppendieck and Poppendieck, Lean Software Development (2003) · Evolutionary architecture

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::15 Evolutionary Architecture
notes.front: What is Big Design Up Front (BDUF), and why do Agile approaches reject it?
notes.back: Completing a detailed design before implementation starts. It commits to decisions at the point of least knowledge and delays feedback. The alternative is not 'no design' but just enough design, continued throughout.
notes.source: Evolutionary architecture

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::15 Evolutionary Architecture
notes.front: What does just enough architecture mean in a risk-driven approach?
notes.back: Spend architecture effort in proportion to risk: identify the biggest risks, apply only the techniques that reduce them, and stop when the remaining risk is acceptable.
notes.source: Fairbanks, Just Enough Software Architecture (2010) · Evolutionary architecture

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::15 Evolutionary Architecture
notes.front: Coupling versus cohesion: what does good modular design aim for?
notes.back: Low coupling: modules depend on each other as little as possible. High cohesion: the things inside a module belong together and change together.
notes.source: Evolutionary architecture

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::15 Evolutionary Architecture
notes.front: What is the strangler fig pattern?
notes.back: Replacing a legacy system gradually: new functionality is built alongside it and calls are routed to the new parts one at a time, until the old system has nothing left to do and can be removed.
notes.source: Fowler, StranglerFigApplication (2004) · Evolutionary architecture

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::15 Evolutionary Architecture
notes.front: What is a walking skeleton?
notes.back: A minimal end-to-end implementation that connects all the main architectural components and can be built, deployed and tested automatically, before any of them has real functionality.
notes.source: Cockburn, Crystal Clear (2004) · Evolutionary architecture

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::15 Evolutionary Architecture
notes.front: What is a modular monolith?
notes.back: A system deployed as one unit but structured internally as well-separated modules with explicit interfaces and their own data. It gives most of the design benefits of microservices without the operational cost of distribution.
notes.source: Evolutionary architecture

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::15 Evolutionary Architecture
notes.text: The four levels of the C4 model for describing software architecture are {{c1::Context, Containers, Components and Code}}.
notes.extra: Each level zooms in on the previous one.
notes.source: Brown, c4model.com · Evolutionary architecture

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::15 Evolutionary Architecture
notes.front: What was Amazon's Application Programming Interface (API) mandate, and why does it matter architecturally?
notes.back: An internal rule from around 2002: every team must expose its data and functionality through service interfaces, with no other form of inter-team access, and design those interfaces to be externalisable. It forced loose coupling and made team autonomy possible.
notes.source: Evolutionary architecture

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::15 Evolutionary Architecture
notes.front: What does Gregor Hohpe's architect elevator metaphor say about the architect's role?
notes.back: Architects create value by riding between the engine room (where technology is built) and the penthouse (where strategy is set), connecting the levels and translating between them.
notes.source: Hohpe, The Software Architect Elevator (2020) · Evolutionary architecture

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::15 Evolutionary Architecture
notes.front: What changes in the role of the architect in an Agile organisation?
notes.back: From producing up-front designs and approving others' work to working with teams: setting direction and guardrails, making trade-offs visible, coaching, and staying hands-on enough to get feedback from running systems.
notes.source: Evolutionary architecture

notes.deck: Agile Architecture::15 Evolutionary Architecture
notes.front: How does real options thinking apply to architecture?
notes.back: Modularity and reversible decisions buy options: the right, but not the obligation, to change later. Options are worth more the higher the uncertainty, so investing in changeability pays most where the future is least clear.
notes.source: Evolutionary architecture
